entry: Iraqi militant leader and founder of the [[Islamic State]] (IS). He became emir of the group in 2010 and, after IS declared a [[Caliphate|caliphate]] in 2014, proclaimed himself caliph. IS captured substantial territory in [[Iraq]] and [[Syria]] and directed mass suicide bombings, executions and the enslavement of Yazidi women and children. IS lost that territory during his tenure. He killed himself by detonating a suicide vest during a U.S. raid in Syria's Idlib Province. IS named Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi as his successor.

Persian physician, philosopher and alchemist of the Islamic Golden Age. Born in Ray, near [[Tehran]], he practiced medicine in [[Baghdad]] and served as chief physician of hospitals in Baghdad and Ray. He was an early proponent of experimental medicine and, with Thābit ibn Qurra, among the first physicians to distinguish clinically between smallpox and measles. He is credited with more than 200 works, including the medical encyclopedia *Ḥāwī* (*Continens*), completed by his pupils after his death and first translated into Latin in 1279. He is described as the father of [[Pediatrics|pediatrics]]. In philosophy he accorded reason a particularly high status and was critical of prophethood and revelation. His doctrine of five 'eternal principles' survives only in fragments, known largely through the reports of hostile writers.

Capital city of the [[United Arab Emirates]] (UAE) and of the emirate of Abu Dhabi (urban pop., 2023 est.: 2,500,000). The city occupies a T-shaped island in the [[Persian Gulf]] off the central-western coast of the UAE, and most of the city and emirate lie on the mainland. Abu Dhabi and five other emirates formed the federation on December 2, 1971, with Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan as its first president. The city houses federal government offices and is home to the president, a member of the Al Nahyan family. Oil and gas reserves transformed it into a large, developed metropolis and a major [[Commerce|commerce]] centre. The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, based in the city, is estimated to manage about US$1 trillion in assets, the world's third-largest sovereign wealth fund. The emirate accounts for about two-thirds of the roughly $503 billion UAE economy.

headword: Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse
sort_key: abu ghraib torture and prisoner abuse
entry: U.S. military scandal over the abuse of detainees at Abu Ghraib prison in [[Iraq]], in 2003–04. Army and [[Central Intelligence Agency]] personnel committed physical and sexual abuse, [[Torture|torture]] and rape of detainees and killed one detainee. Photographs published by CBS News in April 2004 caused international outrage. The George W. Bush administration described the abuses as isolated incidents, a view disputed by the Red Cross, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, who argued they formed part of a wider pattern. Eleven soldiers were court-martialed and convicted.

Muslim scholar, jurist and theologian, eponymous founder of the Hanafi school of [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] jurisprudence. The Hanafi school is the most widely practiced Sunni school, predominating in [[Central Asia]], South Asia, [[Turkey]], Africa, the Balkans, Russia and parts of the Arab world. In his youth he studied in [[Mecca]] and [[Medina]], and he later became a leading religious authority in Kufa. His school used analogy (*qiyās*), juristic preference (*istiḥsān*) and personal judgment (*raʾy*) to resolve new legal problems. He never held the post of qadi (judge) and suffered punishment and imprisonment under both the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]] and the Abbasids for his independent views. He died in prison in [[Baghdad]]. His students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani became celebrated jurists, and most adherents of his school later also followed the Maturidi school of theology.

Persian revolutionary and military commander who was central to the Abbasid Revolution. The Abbasid leadership sent him to organize missionary activity in [[Khorasan]], and in 747 he opened the armed phase of the revolt there, rapidly seizing Merv. He then directed the Abbasid advance across the [[Iranian plateau]] and into the [[Levant]], which brought down the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] and established the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. He served as governor of Khorasan. The second Abbasid caliph, al-Mansur, ordered his execution, alleging crypto-Zoroastrian sympathies; the charge was likely baseless. His death provoked unrest across Greater Iran, where he was venerated as a martyr for centuries.

Classical Arabic poet and the foremost representative of *muhdath* ('modern') poetry, which developed in the early [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. Of mixed Arab and Persian heritage, he was born in the Ahvaz region and studied the Qur'an, [[Hadith]] and grammar in Basra and Kufa, where he was first apprenticed to the poet Waliba ibn al-Hubab. He earned the favor of the Abbasid caliphs [[Harun al-Rashid]] and al-Amin. He is best known for his wine poetry (*khamriyyāt*) and his *Diwan*, a collection that explored religion, pleasure and homoeroticism. Some 500 of his erotic lyric poems and fragments survive. He also appears several times in *One Thousand and One Nights*.

Capital of [[Nigeria]], situated at the country's geographic midpoint within the Federal Capital Territory (pop., 2006: 776,298). It replaced [[Lagos]] as the capital on December 12, 1991. The site was chosen in the early 1970s as neutral among the country's ethnic groups and to relieve the overcrowding of Lagos. A military decree of February 4, 1976, began the move, but economic and political instability delayed construction, and the early stages were not complete until the late 1980s. The city is dominated by Aso Rock, a 400-metre monolith, south of which lie the Presidential Complex, the National Assembly and the Supreme Court. According to the United Nations, Abuja grew by 139.7% between 2000 and 2010. It joined the [[UNESCO]] Global Network of Learning Cities in 2016.

Flat area of the deep [[Ocean|ocean]] floor, usually at depths of 3,000 to 6,000 metres. Lying generally between the foot of a continental rise and a [[Mid-ocean ridge]], abyssal plains cover more than 50% of Earth's surface and are among the flattest and least explored regions on the planet. They form as [[Plate tectonics|seafloor spreading]] creates new oceanic crust and fine sediments, mainly clay and silt, bury its uneven surface. Turbidity currents carry much of this sediment from continental margins. Metallic nodules containing manganese, iron, nickel, cobalt and copper are common in some areas. Because of their vast size, the plains are believed to be major reservoirs of [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]] and to influence ocean carbon cycling. Oxygen is scarce, and water pressure can reach about 750 times atmospheric pressure, so the plains were not recognized as distinct features until the late 1940s and remain poorly explored.

Breed of domestic cat with a distinctive ticked tabby coat, in which each hair is banded with several colors. Abyssinians are lean, active and highly social cats that do well in multi-cat households but are not lap cats. The name refers to Abyssinia, now [[Ethiopia]], though genetic studies place the breed's origins in [[Southeast Asia]] and [[Europe]]. The breed was recognized in 1929 by the Governing Council of the Cat Fancy. After a feline leukaemia virus outbreak, it nearly died out in the United Kingdom after World War II and was rebuilt with imported cats.

Genus of about 1,084 species of shrubs and trees in the [[Fabaceae|pea family]]. Known as wattles, the genus is now mostly limited to species from [[Australia]], with others from New Guinea and [[Southeast Asia]]. Many mature plants have phyllodes, flattened leaf stalks that function as leaves. Gum arabic comes from African species such as *Acacia senegal*, and bark rich in [[Tannin|tannins]] is used in leather and dyes. Several species have been introduced to other parts of the world, and two million hectares of commercial plantations have been established.

Style of painting and sculpture produced under the influence of European academies of art. It originated in Italy in the mid-16th century, when the first academy was founded in Florence in 1563 under the influence of [[Giorgio Vasari]]. Academies were established to replace medieval artists' guilds and emphasized the emulation of established masters and the [[Classicism|classical]] tradition. The style reached its height in the 19th century, after the Napoleonic Wars, when the standards of the French Académie des Beaux-Arts combined elements of [[Neoclassicism]] and [[Romanticism]]. [[Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres]] was a key figure. Academic artists favored idealized, polished history paintings drawn from antiquity, mythology and Orientalist subjects over everyday scenes. [[Realism (arts)|Realism]] and [[Impressionism]] rejected it, and by World War I it had largely lost favor, though it regained some appreciation after the late 20th century.

Qualification awarded to a student on completing a course of study in higher education. Degrees are commonly structured as undergraduate and postgraduate. The most common undergraduate qualification is the [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor's degree]], although some systems also offer associate or foundation degrees. Postgraduate degrees include the engineer's degree, the [[Master's degree|master's degree]] and the doctorate. The doctorate grew out of the *licentia docendi* (license to teach) granted by medieval European universities. The earliest doctoral degrees were in [[Theology|theology]], [[Law]] and [[Medicine]]. In the United Kingdom, honours degrees are divided into first, upper second (2.1), lower second (2.2) and third class.

Periodical publication in which scholarship from a particular academic discipline is published, usually written by researchers rather than staff writers. Research articles nearly always undergo [[Peer review|peer review]] by competent contemporaries. Content usually takes the form of original research, review articles and book reviews. Most journals are highly specialized, though journals such as [[Science (journal)|Science]] and [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] cover many scientific fields. As of 2012, more than 28,100 active academic journals were in publication. The *Journal des sçavans* appeared in [[France]] on January 5, 1665, and the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society* in [[England]] the same year. Because publication counts influence academic promotion, researchers face pressure to publish frequently, an environment known as publish or perish.

Annual awards for artistic and technical merit in film, presented in Hollywood by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) and known as the Oscars. The Oscar statuette depicts a knight in the Art Deco style. The first ceremony was held on May 16, 1929, honoring films from 1927 and 1928. The 1930 ceremony was the first broadcast by radio, and the 1953 ceremony was the first to be televised. The Oscars are widely considered the most prestigious awards in the film industry. The Emmy, Tony and [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] awards were modeled on them. In 2002 the first Academy Award for Best Animated Feature went to *Shrek*. The ceremony will move to [[YouTube]] in 2029.

Colony of [[New France]] in northeastern North America, including parts of what are now the Maritime provinces, the Gaspé Peninsula and Maine to the Kennebec River. Settlers came mainly from southwestern France, and the first capital, Port-Royal, was established in 1605. Britain conquered the colony in 1710 during Queen Anne's War, and the territory was later divided into British colonies. Between 1755 and 1764 about 11,500 Acadians were expelled during the [[Seven Years' War]]. Survivors dispersed to [[Louisiana]], where their descendants are known as Cajuns, and to other regions.

Extinct paraphyletic class of jawed fishes, often called spiny sharks. Acanthodians were shark-shaped, with paired fins and bony spines supporting all fins except the tail, but they are not true sharks. They form a grade of fishes basal to [[Chondrichthyes]], the group that includes living sharks, rays and chimaeras. Their skeletons were largely cartilage, so fossil spines and scales are often all that survives, and the scales are used to date sedimentary rock. The earliest unequivocal fossils date from the [[Silurian]]. Freshwater species flourished in the [[Devonian]], and the last survivors died out in the [[Permian]], about 250 million years ago, as bony fishes came to dominate.

Rate of change of velocity, a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction. Acceleration measures how quickly an object's velocity changes in speed or direction. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval, *a* = Δ*v*/Δ*t*. Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of [[Velocity|velocity]] with respect to time, and so the second derivative of position. Its SI unit is the metre per second squared (m/s²). By Newton's second law, net acceleration is proportional to the net [[Force]] on an object and inversely proportional to its [[Mass]]. Tangential acceleration changes speed along the direction of motion, while radial (centripetal) acceleration changes the direction of velocity in circular motion.

Distinctive way of pronouncing a language, associated with a region, social class, ethnic group or individual. Accents differ in voice quality, the pronunciation of vowels and consonants, stress and prosody, while a [[Dialect|dialect]] also includes differences in grammar and vocabulary. Accents develop as communities become isolated and as contact between groups changes; in North America they formed from the mixing of many ethnic backgrounds and the pronunciations of British settlers. Children acquire accents early, and accents remain relatively malleable until the early twenties. Speakers who deviate from prestige norms are often stereotyped, and research has found that accented speech can disadvantage speakers in hiring and performance ratings.

Genus of birds of prey in the family Accipitridae, some species of which are called sparrowhawks. Accipiters have short, broad, rounded wings and long tails that aid maneuvering in woodland, along with long legs and sharp talons. Females are larger than males. They usually ambush small birds and mammals after a short chase. The genus was introduced by Mathurin Jacques Brisson in 1760, with the Eurasian sparrowhawk (*Accipiter nisus*) as type species; the name is [[Latin]] for 'hawk'. The traditional genus, which once contained about 50 species, proved non-monophyletic in molecular studies. A 2024 revision moved many species into other genera, leaving nine in *Accipiter*.

Bellows-driven free-reed instrument that combines a melody keyboard and an accompaniment section in one body. Air pushed through the bellows passes tuned brass or steel reeds, producing sound. The right hand usually plays the melody on keys or buttons, while the left plays bass notes and chords. The basic form is believed to have been invented in [[Berlin]] in 1822, and the first patent for an instrument called the accordion was granted in 1829 to Cyrill Demian in [[Vienna]]. Migration from Europe spread the instrument widely; it is used in popular music in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico, and in folk, [[Jazz]] and klezmer styles. Related instruments include the [[Harmonica]], concertina and bandoneon.

Process of recording and processing information about economic entities such as [[Business|businesses]] and corporations. Accounting measures the results of economic activity and conveys them to stakeholders, including investors, creditors, management and regulators. Its main branches are financial, management, [[Tax|tax]] and cost accounting. The recording of transactions is called bookkeeping, most commonly in double-entry form, which developed in medieval [[Venice]] and is usually attributed to the mathematician Luca Pacioli, whose *Summa de arithmetica* was published in 1494. Financial statements in the United States are prepared under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). Accounting dates to ancient [[Mesopotamia]], where it was closely tied to writing, counting and money.

Capital and largest city of [[Ghana]], on the coast of the [[Gulf of Guinea]] (pop., 2021: 1,782,150). That figure covers the city's territory before 2008, when it was divided into 13 districts; the Accra Metropolitan District alone had 284,124 residents. Formed from settlements around British, Dutch and Danish forts, Accra was capital of the British Gold Coast from 1877 to 1957. It is the economic and administrative hub of the Greater Accra Region, the anchor of a metropolitan area of about 4 million people. In 2020 the Globalization and World Cities Research Network designated it a 'Gamma −' [[Global city|global city]]. The name derives from the Akan word *Nkran*, meaning 'ants'.

Two measures of observational error. Accuracy is how close a measurement or set of measurements is to the true value, and precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. Precision describes random error, quantified by the [[Standard deviation|standard deviation]] of a set of results. In its more common sense, accuracy describes systematic error, or bias. The International Organization for Standardization defines *trueness* as the closeness of the mean of many results to the reference value. A measurement system may be accurate, precise, both or neither. Increasing sample size improves precision but does not correct a systematic error, while removing the error improves accuracy without changing precision. A measurement system is considered valid only if it is both accurate and precise.

Westernmost province of [[Indonesia]], at the northern end of [[Sumatra]] island (pop., 2025: 5,626,000). Its capital and largest city is Banda Aceh. Aceh has special autonomous status and is the only Indonesian province to officially integrate [[Sharia]], or Islamic law. Islam reached the region around 1250, and the Aceh Sultanate was a powerful state in the [[Strait of Malacca]] in the early 17th century. Aceh has a history of resistance to outside control, including against the [[Dutch East Indies]]. It has substantial oil and [[Natural gas|natural gas]] resources. The [[2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami]] struck close to its coast, and about 170,000 Indonesians were killed or went missing. The disaster helped precipitate a 2005 peace agreement with the separatist Free Aceh Movement.
